History:
- Presenting complaint: Soreness and cracking of skin on the hands, predominantly the palms; dryness noted on legs but milder.
- Onset/duration: Symptoms began about 3–4 months ago; persistent and gradually worse, recently painful and affecting work.
- Progression/context: Works as a hotel housekeeper; occasional poor glove use; possible correlation with cleaning products.
- Associated symptoms: Itching of the palms; occasional bleeding with scratching; no fever, nausea, vomiting, abdominal or urinary symptoms.
- Triggers/working conditions: Exposure to cleaning products; inconsistent glove use; recently changed job (4 months ago).

Past Medical History:
- Diabetes mellitus type 2, on metformin.
- No known skin diseases (eczema/dermatitis denied).
- Allergies: None.
- Medications: Metformin; OTC E45 cream previously tried with no relief; antihistamine tried with no relief.
- Family history: Diabetes.

Physical Examination:
- Findings not explicitly documented in transcript; patient reports: dry, cracked palms with itching; bleeding only with scratching.
- No systemic symptoms reported.

Impression:
- Dermatitis, likely contact dermatitis related to occupational exposure to cleaning products; palms predominantly affected.

Management Plan:
- Avoid triggers: wear gloves at all times when cleaning.
- Topical therapy: corticosteroid cream to reduce inflammation.
- Emollient therapy: stronger moisturizers; apply to affected areas 3–4 times daily for the next couple of weeks.
- Follow-up: if no improvement within 10–14 days or if worsening/spreading occurs, return for reevaluation and possible alternative treatments.
- Medications: Prescription for topical corticosteroid cream and an emollient to be sent to pharmacy (dose/route/frequency not documented in transcript).
- Patient education: discuss potential correlation with occupational exposure and importance of protective gloves.

Patient Summary:
A 45-year-old woman with diabetes presents with a several-month history of dry, cracked palmar skin and itching, worse with occupational cleaning duties. Likely contact dermatitis related to cleaning products. Plan includes glove use, topical steroid, and emollients with follow-up in 1–2 weeks or sooner if worsening.

Key Takeaways:
- Wear gloves during cleaning at all times to reduce triggers.
- Use prescribed topical corticosteroid and strong emollient as directed; moisturize frequently.
- Return for follow-up in about 10–14 days if not improved or sooner if symptoms worsen.

Next Steps:
- Initiate prescription for topical corticosteroid cream and emollient; obtain from pharmacy.
- Reassess in 1–2 weeks; consider additional therapies if no improvement or if symptoms spread/worsen.

- Missing elements: No documented vitals (BP, HR, temp, etc.); no formal physical examination details beyond patient report; no explicit medication reconciliation beyond metformin; no documented allergies other than “none.”
- Internal conflicts: None identified.
- Transcript quality: Clear; some typical clinical details inferred from patient report (no explicit exam findings provided).
